opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift is that so much of science today is already computational, even in fields that people think of as very hands-on, like biology or chemistry. A huge fraction of a scientist's time goes into writing analysis scripts, wrangling data from instruments, setting up pipelines, debugging someone else's code from a paper three years ago. That's not the part anyone went into science to do, but it's the part that often determines how fast you can move.

So where I see Codex becoming foundational is in taking on that layer. You can describe what you want in plain language: "take these sequencing files, run the standard quality control, align them, and give me the differential expression results with a few plots." Then it can actually go do the work, iterate when something breaks, and come back with something you can inspect. That lowers the barrier for a bench scientist who isn't a trained programmer, and it speeds up the computational folks who are.

The other piece I'm excited about is reproducibility. When an agent is doing the work, there's a natural record of every step: the code, the parameters, the decisions. That makes it much easier to share, audit, and rerun analyses, which science has struggled with for a long time.

And longer term, as these systems get better at reasoning over longer horizons, they can move beyond executing a workflow toward helping design one: suggesting the right statistical test, flagging a confounder, proposing the next experiment. The scientist stays in the driver's seat, setting the questions and judging the results, but the loop between having an idea and seeing whether the data supports it gets a lot shorter. That's really the foundation I'm hoping we build.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that science has always been bottlenecked less by ideas and more by the grind between an idea and a result. You have a hypothesis, and then there's this long tail of work: wrangling data formats, writing the analysis script, getting the simulation to compile, tracking down why the plot looks wrong at three in the morning. Most of that isn't science, it's plumbing. And Codex is really good at plumbing.

So the first thing we see is just compression of that loop. A biologist who has a question about a dataset can describe what they want, and instead of spending a week learning pandas or waiting on a collaborator who knows how to code, they get a working pipeline in an afternoon. That changes who gets to ask computational questions at all. The surface area of who can do computational science gets a lot bigger.

But the more interesting part, the part where I think "foundation" is the right word, is when you move from one-off scripts to something that lives alongside the research. Codex can read a whole repo, understand the conventions a lab has built up over years, and extend them without breaking them. It can take a method from a paper and implement it against your data. It can run experiments, look at the output, notice something's off, and go back and fix it. That's less like a tool and more like a junior collaborator who never gets tired and has read every library's documentation.

And then there's reproducibility, which honestly is where I get most excited. So much of science today is irreproducible not because people are dishonest but because the code was a mess and the environment was never captured. When the agent is doing the work, you get the whole trace: what it ran, what it changed, why. That's a record you can hand to a reviewer or a future student. I think in a few years we'll look back and find it strange that the computational part of a paper was ever a black box.

I'd add one caveat, because it matters. Codex doesn't replace scientific judgment. It'll happily implement a flawed analysis beautifully. The scientists getting the most out of it are the ones who treat it like a very capable colleague: give it context, check its reasoning, push back when something looks too clean. The foundation is the agent doing the heavy lifting, but the direction still has to come from someone who understands what question is actually worth asking.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunity is for Codex to help connect the different parts of scientific work. A researcher might start with a question, write code to analyze a dataset, run an experiment, and then use the results to decide what to investigate next. There’s a lot of work involved in moving between those steps.

Codex could help with that whole loop: translating an idea into an analysis, debugging the code, and making it easier to reproduce and build on the results. That would let scientists spend more time thinking about the question and interpreting the evidence.

But getting code to run isn’t the same as getting the science right. To become a foundation for these workflows, it needs to make its assumptions and changes easy to inspect, support validation, and keep researchers in control of the scientific decisions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is for Codex to help connect the steps of scientific work. A researcher has a question, but getting to an answer often involves writing code, cleaning data, running an analysis, and figuring out why something failed. If Codex can help across those steps, researchers can spend more time thinking about the science.

And the important part is making that work inspectable and reproducible. What code ran? What assumptions went into the analysis? Can someone else reproduce the result? The scientist still has to judge whether the question and the evidence make sense. But Codex could make it much easier to turn an idea into an experiment, learn from the result, and try again.
